abstract: [bullet] Variation in macroevolutionary dynamics, from rapid radiations to slower evolutionary change, can shape multiple facets of biodiversity. However, whether the contributions of contrasting macroevolutionary dynamics to biodiversity differ across timescales, and whether shifts in abiotic niches drive recent radiations, remain open questions in evolutionary biology. [bullet] Using the megadiverse genus Mimosa, we investigate the contribution of contrasting macroevolutionary dynamics to biodiversity and what drives these dynamics at shallow timescales. We combined species-diversity, morphological, and abiotic niche data to estimate biodiversity metrics, infer macroevolutionary rates, and test the role of abiotic niche lability as a driver of radiation-like dynamics. [bullet] We found that Mimosa clades are distributed across a continuum of macroevolutionary dynamics, with those clades resembling radiations clearly contributing to most diversity and disparity, but not niche breadth. Moreover, rates of altitudinal and edaphic niche change were associated with diversification, whereas rates of change in these two niche dimensions, along with climatic niche change, were associated with morphological evolution. Finally, the contribution of radiations to biodiversity seemed to decrease toward the present. [bullet] Overall, our work highlights that both relatively rapid and slow lineage diversification underlie the multifaceted nature of biodiversity and reinforces the role of abiotic niche lability in plant diversification.
